=== trail
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.
=== quote
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

**Q1. May the compiled checker refuse an object that inherits an abstract method from one trait and its body from another?**

- **Primer.** A functional method has `self` among its parameters and is called like a function, `pick(x)`. A trait can leave one abstract, with no body. Example:
  - `trait A  pick(self): String  end` is abstract.
  - `trait B  pick(self): String = "b"  end` has a body.
  - `object O extends { A, B } end` declares no `pick` of its own.
- **What happens today.** The compiled path accepts `O` and runs B's body, even for a call typed by A. Walk stops with an internal error (row 572).   - Accept: the team's own abstract-method check, and Scala.
  - For row 727's shape, a method declared twice in one trait, all of them refuse.
- **Why it's yours.** Batch 8's judge left the default at "don't read them" (review-queue item 62). Changing that default is a split of the sources, not something the principles settle.

The options:
1. **(a) Read them.** The checker refuses both shapes, and rows 572 and 727 close. Rung K builds it.
2. **(b) Leave them unread.** Both rows stay open, and rung K shrinks to row 720 alone.

How they weigh:
- (a) turns a later crash and a silently chosen body into a checker error. It gives up Scala's way of letting a sibling trait supply the body.
- If the library itself uses that pattern, rung K stops and reports rather than land.
- (a) is one condition in one filter, so it's easy to reverse.
- (b) changes nothing and keeps both holes.

I recommend (a).

  - the same name;
  - the self parameter at the same position;
  - the same parameter type, the self parameter's apart;
  - an equal return type (or, for Scala's full rule, a subtype).

A sentence is needed, and the text already has it as a draft-only note (`traits.tex:653-655`): "Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not accessible." ------
We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.



-----

When a method declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{method definition}.
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method: a method definition with the same name and the self parameter (if any)
at the same position whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self
parameter, is that of the abstract method declaration, or definitions whose
parameter types are subtypes of it and together cover it
(\secref{internal-types}), or it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said only that
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.
----
Object declarations declare both object values and \objecttypes.
Object declarations extend a
set of traits from which they inherit methods.
An object declaration inherits the
concrete methods of its supertraits and must include a definition for every
method declared but not defined by its supertraits.
Especially, an object declaration must not include abstract methods
(discussed in \secref{methods});
it must define all abstract methods inherited from its supertraits.
It is also allowed to define overloaded declarations of concrete methods
inherited from its supertraits.

1	<!-- How climb batch 16's Q1 (an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another) reached the curator, why it went toward Scala's way and back, what the probe found, what the detour cost, and what changes; written 2026-10-15 by the coordinating session at the curator's word ("Let's make sure we have a proper report recorded from this exercise."). -->
     2	
     3	# Q1 of climb batch 16: the detour toward Scala's way
     4	
     5	## In short
     6	
     7	- **The question.** May the compiled checker refuse `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives it a body, and `O` declares none of its own (rows 572 and 727)?
     8	- **The answer.** Refuse it (P-149), the curator's word of 06:23 UTC: the specification's text and the type group's later calculus refuse it, and the revival does not bend Fortress toward another language for a convenience.
     9	- **The detour.** The ask put to the curator led him toward Scala's way, which accepts `O`. He pre-recorded it, then learnt that the specification refuses `O`, and took the refusal.
    10	- **Its cost.** About 1.7M tokens written: the probe 0.56M, and this session 1.17M, nearly all of it two rewrites of its 550K context into the cache after the VM restart and after a gap of nearly two hours.
    11	- **The causes.** The ask did not say first what the designers' text says and which way it points. It named a peer language's behaviour as if it were an option of equal standing. It used the record's shorthand. And the fact that would decide the question, whether the library uses the shape, was not measured before the ask.
    12	
    13	## The question
    14	
    15	A functional method has `self` among its parameters and is called like a function, `pick(x)`. A trait may leave one abstract, with no body:
    16	
    17	```
    18	trait A  pick(self): String  end           (* abstract *)
    19	trait B  pick(self): String = "b"  end     (* a body *)
    20	object O extends { A, B } end              (* no pick of its own *)
    21	```
    22	
    23	Today the compiled path accepts `O` and runs `B`'s body, because its overloading check skips a component's own abstract functional methods (`OverloadingChecker.scala:139-141`). Walk refuses `O` at load (F-142). Separately, an abstract and a concrete declaration of one method in one trait pass the checker and crash the code generator (row 727).
    24	
    25	## How it went, in UTC
    26	
    27	- **01:08 to 01:37.** Batch 16's planner drafted Q1 with the default "refuse" (rung K builds it), and listed the sources: the specification, the type group's rules, the team's dotted-method check and Java refuse; the team's abstract-method check and Scala accept. Its brief told it to run no new probe, so the record left the library's use of the shape to rung K's own run.
    28	- **01:38 to 02:11.** The Fable review agreed that Q1 is the curator's.
    29	- **02:13.** The coordinator put Q1 to the curator. The ask used the record's words ("batch 8's judge", "item 62", "read them", "leave them unread"), gave the sources as a split without saying that the specification's text refuses `O`, and gave as the refusal's cost that it "gives up Scala's way of letting a sibling trait supply the body".
    30	- **04:18.** The curator found the ask unreadable past its primer, leaned to Scala's way if it had a clean resolution, and asked why the library's use of the shape had not been measured, "the most important factor for the decision".
    31	- **04:19.** The coordinator launched the probe (`perf-probes/abstract-sibling-body/`).
    32	- **06:10 to 06:13.** While it ran, the curator pre-recorded Scala's way, unless hard evidence against it surfaced (P-149, first form).
    33	- **06:14.** The curator, who had listened to the ask in a car, asked whether the specification declared this way. The coordinator told him that it refuses `O`, and held P-149.
    34	- **06:17.** The probe reported. The curator asked why the work had gone toward Scala's way at all, if the specification and the implementations agreed. They did not agree: the compiled path accepts `O`, walk refuses it, and one of the team's own checks (`AbstractMethodChecker.scala:94-107`) counts an inherited body as the implementation. Scala had entered only as the coordinator's comparison.
    35	- **06:23.** The curator took the refusal.
    36	
    37	## What the probe found
    38	
    39	From `explorations/perf-probes/abstract-sibling-body/REPORT.md`:
    40	
    41	- **Neither library uses the shape.** No type in the one library or the compiler's library inherits an abstract functional method and a sibling's body without providing their meet. With the checker's filter lifted, the count and distance stages are unchanged.
    42	- **Scala's way is buildable for equal types.** It takes one exemption in the checker and two edits in walk, and nothing in the code generator. It needs two passages of the specification rewritten. A narrower return type or an api boundary reaches code-generator defects (rows 732 to 735).
    43	- **The designers' word refuses `O`.** The specification's text refuses it. The type group's Welterweight calculus (2012) refuses it too, the work behind P-147. POPL 2019 has no abstract methods. Java refuses `O`; Scala accepts it.
    44	- **The record had stale claims.** Walk refuses `O` at load and no longer stops at a call. The compiler's library declares abstract functional methods in its api (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37-40`). Welterweight admits an abstract and a concrete declaration at one domain, so "every source refuses row 727" is overstated.
    45	
    46	## What changes
    47	
    48	- **P-149** records the refusal and the curator's rule behind it: other languages are consulted only to reconcile a conflict between the designers' earlier and later choices.
    49	- **Climb batch 16's rung K** stays as drafted. Before the splice, its record takes the probe's corrections: walk's refusal at load, the compiler's library's abstract api declarations, and the wording on row 727.
    50	- **The ledger** has the probe's four rows, 732 to 735.
    51	- **For the `coordinator` skill** (held for the skill writer):
    52	  - An ask states first what the designers' text and their later word say, and which way they point. A peer language's behaviour enters only where the designers' earlier and later choices conflict.
    53	  - The coordinator runs the probe that a planner names for a question before putting the question to the curator.
    54	  - The ask's plain words are already a rule. Here it was not followed.
    55	- **This session's cost of a cold turn.** With its context near 580K, a turn after an hour's gap or a restart rewrites about 0.55M into the cache. A compaction before a long gap cuts that.
**Standard 1.** The No Duplicates Rule (`advanced/overloading.tex:548-549`), the Meet Rule over what a type provides (`basic/traits.tex:580-581`) and an object's duty to define what it inherits abstract (`traits.tex:628-633`): built. Where an error is reported, the text is silent.

**Standard 2.** The team's dotted check reads abstract dotted methods with no body filter (`OverloadingChecker.scala:170-172`): the precedent. The placement is new machinery. javac and scalac report at the use (call 4).

**Standard 3.**
- **P-149** is built: rows 727, 572 and 734 are closed. Both libraries compile, and no site comes.
- **The refusals reach beyond the named rows** (`SKEPTIC.md` section 6). Each one is the Meet or Return Type Rule, applied as it was to the dotted twin:
  - row 734's swapped face;
  - a trait that inherits both;
  - a trait that redeclares at an unrelated return type, which failed verification on the base;
  - an abstract pair at two `self` positions over `ZZ32`, which walk runs (row 698's mechanism).
- **Call 4**, "reported at the call", is built and extended twice:
  - once for each call: the skeptic's contested fix, upheld by the judge (`JUDGE.md` section 3);
  - for every well-formedness error on a type met outside its expression, not only a broken bound: an unbound type, an arity, a size, and errors the base printed at 'Type checker generated.:0:0' (`REPORT.md` section 9). `GenTest5`, outside the suites, went from 32 errors to 36.

  The second reach is not before him.
- **Call 5** is built: operators stay unread, and row 726 is still the code generator's.
- **Found, and not P-149's case:** row 739, the top-level set, which reads only declarations with a body.

**Verdict: in the spirit.** The placement's reach goes on his list.

- **737**: no line of its own. Proposed: batch 17's checker rung, first.
- **738**, the per-provider message calls an object 'trait' (`OverloadingChecker.scala:338`, pinned by `XXXDottedMethodMeetAbstractSibling`): no PLAN line. Proposed: batch 17's checker rung.
- **739**: the review list (K.skeptic.2). Proposed: batch 17's checker rung.
- **740 and 741**: the review list (W.skeptic.2). No rung until he answers.
- **742**, walk loads two generic declarations with equal domains: no PLAN line. Proposed: the next walk rung, beside rows 549 and 159.

### What the record listed for him, and PLAN lacks

- **Q1's answer** is settled by P-149. P-149's "Still to build: climb batch 16's rung K, rows 572 and 727" is built: cut it with `record.py`. Review-queue item 62 and its line at `PLAN.md:269` are answered: move them.

Proposed: one entry, "Calls 1 to 6 of climb batch 16, as built", default as built. Calls 1, 2, 3 and 5 are for his sight; call 4 goes with K.judge.1's entry, and call 6 with gather.2's.
- **"Points the batch lists for you, not questions"** (`CLIMB-BATCH-16.md:88-93`) have no entry. Proposed: one entry, "Points of climb batch 16, for his sight", default as landed:
  - team lines changed: H's 936 and 21 hash lines; W's `forIf` and its lines in `OverloadedFunction.java`, the shortcut among them; K's functional set, the team's line 133 of 2012;

Yes, you have it now. This was a review item: a decision a batch made on its own, put on your list so you can see whether it bent the language. I put it to you as if it blocked the next batch. That's the root cause.

**How it came up.** Not from `NatParam`. A different rung of batch 13 made walk's `override` check strict, so that walk refuses an `override` that replaces nothing. The rung's first version refused one program shape that walk had always run. The skeptic, the agent that checks each rung's work, found this. It chose to keep walk running that program and listed the choice for you.

**The idea, in concrete cases.** Conditional extension means a type gains an ability only when its parts have it.
- **Lists, ordered when their elements are:**
  ```
  trait List[\E\]
      extends LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\], E\]
      where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }
  ```
  - `<|1, 2|> < <|1, 3|>` is true: numbers are ordered, so lists of numbers are too.
  - `<|"b"|> < <|"a", "z"|>` is false, compared word by word.
  - A list of functions is still a list. You can append to it or map over it, but `<` on it is a static error, because functions have no order.
- **Vectors, addable when their elements are:**
  ```
  trait Vec[\T\]
      extends AdditiveGroup[\Vec[\T\]\]
      where { T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\] }
  ```
  - Two vectors of `ZZ32` add element by element.
  - A vector of strings exists and can be indexed, but `+` on it is an error.

**The question, in those cases.** Inside `List`, the definition of `<` compares the elements one by one, using the elements' own `<`. That's valid only if the checker may assume the condition, "the elements are ordered", while it checks that definition. The batch's choice was yes: inside the conditional part, the condition holds. The other answer would make the definition of `<` an error, since it would have to work for lists of anything, functions included.

**The nine steps, briefly:**
1. **The type theory.** It's an "if": the list is ordered if its elements are. Inside the "then" part you may use the "if", as in any proof.
2. **The specification** gives only the grammar: each `extends` entry may carry its own `where` clause. It states no rule, and the front matter lists the feature as not yet supported.
3. **The team's later word.** Their 2012 and 2019 type papers don't have the feature. Their farewell post named it as one of three things they wished they'd explored.
4. **The team's library** has no live use. But the specification's text orders a list only when its elements are ordered. That's the team's intent, and the list comparisons error comes from it.
5. **Peers.**
   - Swift: `extension Array: Equatable where Element: Equatable`.
